ion Observation Mission (EU EOM) described the elections as credible and genuinely competitive, noting a revitalised civic space and broad respect for fundamental freedoms during the campaign period.

How have the changes affected political groups?

The political transition has reshaped Bangladesh’s political landscape. The period has seen greater political participation by a range of political actors, including established opposition parties, newly formed political parties and student-led political movements. It has also created opportunities for political parties and civil society organisations to contribute to discussions on governance and institutional reform.

The impact has varied across different political groups. Parties that had previously been in opposition have assumed a more prominent role in political life and electoral politics. At the same time, the Awami League has faced significant legal and operational restrictions.

Has the newly elected BNP government implemented any recommendations from commissions formed under the interim government? If so, what?

The commissions established by the interim government informed a number of ordinances (laws or regulations) and reform proposals across areas including constitutional, electoral, judicial, public administration, police and anti-corruption reform. These recommendations were subsequently considered through the National Consensus Commission process and reflected in the July National Charter.

Following the election, Parliament reviewed 133 ordinances promulgated during the interim period. A special parliamentary committee recommended that 98 ordinances be approved, 15 be amended before enactment, and 20 not be approved in their existing form. Under Bangladesh’s constitutional framework, ordinances not approved by Parliament lapse, although revised legislation may subsequently be introduced through the normal legislative process.

What is the current status of the Awami League (legally, in theory and in practice)?

The Awami League’s political activities were prohibited under measures introduced during the interim administration in 2025, and the party’s registration was cancelled, preventing its participation in the February 2026 parliamentary elections. Parliament subsequently enacted legislation maintaining those restrictions.

The party is not represented in Parliament and is unable to undertake formal political activities in the same manner as registered political parties. However, the Awami League continues to have members, supporters and a recognised political identity.

While the party and its supporters continue to engage in political advocacy and commentary, including through statements from party leaders, online platforms and activities conducted from outside Bangladesh, these activities take place within the context of the legal and operational restrictions currently in force. Public organisational activity within Bangladesh remains limited by those restrictions.

What is the role of the auxiliary organisations (particularly student wings) in political parties?

Auxiliary organisations, including student, youth, labour and professional wings, have long been a feature of Bangladesh’s political landscape. They are typically affiliated with larger political parties and play an important role in political mobilisation, leadership development, advocacy and outreach. Student organisations in particular have often served as an entry point into politics, with many national political leaders beginning their political careers through student activism.

Following the events of 2024, student groups have received increased public attention given the prominent role played by students in the protests that preceded the political transition. The period since then has also seen the emergence of new student-led political initiatives and parties.

Any legal / legislative restrictions on operation for political parties?

Political parties are generally able to organise and participate in political activity within Bangladesh’s legal framework. Political parties remain subject to applicable laws governing registration, elections, public order and political activity.

The restrictions on Awami League are covered in an earlier question.

Are members / supporters of political organisations able to express their views / protest?

The Constitution of Bangladesh provides for freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly. Members and supporters of political parties, civil society organisations and other groups continue to express their views through public statements, meetings, social media, rallies and protests.

Since the political transition of 2024, a broad range of political actors, including established parties, newly formed political groups, student-led movements, religious organisations, civil society groups and issue-based movements have participated in public debate and political activity.

The position of the Awami League is distinct, given the legal restrictions currently in force on the party’s activities. While Awami League leaders, members and supporters continue to express political views, the party is not able to organise and participate in political activities in the same manner as other political parties.

More broadly, domestic and international human rights organisations have reported human rights concerns in relation to detention, politically motivated arrests and prosecutions involving political actors. While many reported cases have involved individuals associated with the former Awami League administration, concerns have also been raised regarding the treatment of political opponents, activists and public figures more generally.

Political demonstrations and rallies continue to take place in Bangladesh. However, there are periodic reports of tensions and clashes between supporters of different political groups.

Version 2.0, October 2026

Executive summary

In July and August 2024, widespread protests resulted in the resignation of Awami League (AL) Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the establishment of an interim government (IG) under the leadership of Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, who was not affiliated to any political party.

On 12 February 2026, Bangladesh held a general election, which was generally considered to be democratic, fair and transparent. The Bangladesh National Party (BNP) received a majority of votes, and leader Tarique Rahman was sworn in as Prime Minister on 17 February 2026. The transition of power was reported to be peaceful. Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI) received the second largest number of votes in the election and are serving within the opposition. The AL were prohibited from running in the elections and remain a banned political party.

District committees have been set up by the Ministry of Home Affairs to review politically motivated cases lodged under the AL regime and, where cases are found to be politically motivated, they are recommended for withdrawal. The Bangladesh police indicated that, so far, around 500,000 individuals have had their cases withdrawn through this process. Members of the BNP and JeI who were previously charged under the AL government on politically motivated grounds have had their convictions overturned.

Leaders, members, and supporters of political groups in Bangladesh are unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state, or from non-state/rogue state actors, on the grounds of their actual or perceived political opinion. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

In general, high profile and senior AL leaders, particularly those who held significant positions in the former government, are likely to face prosecution, rather than persecution, on the grounds of the actions committed under the former government, rather than due to their political opinion.

A person who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a rogue state and/or non-state actor due to their actual or perceived political opinion is likely to obtain protection from the state and is likely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk.

Where a claim from an actual or perceived BNP affiliate, supporter, member or leader, based on a fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors, is refused, it is likely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Other claims based on fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors are unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

All cases must be considered on their individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Assessment

Section updated: 30 September 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights law and policy, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

a person faces a real risk of persecution/serious harm by state and/or non-state actors because of their political or imputed political opinion

the state (or quasi state bodies) can provide effective protection

internal relocation is possible to avoid persecution/serious harm

if refused, a claim is likely or not to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process)).

consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis).

Official – sensitive: Not for disclosure – Start of section

The information on this page has been removed as it is restricted for internal Home Office use.

Official – sensitive: Not for disclosure – End of section

2. Exclusion

2.1.1 Decision makers must consider whether there are serious reasons to apply one (or more) of the exclusion clauses. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

2.1.2 Under the former Awami League (AL) government and during the student quota protests (July-August 2024), members of the security forces and AL members and affiliates have been accused of human rights abuses. The AL’s student wing, the Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL) remains listed as a terrorist organisation under the current BNP government.

2.1.3 If the person is excluded from the Refugee Convention, they will also be excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection (which has a wider range of exclusions than refugee status).

2.1.4 For guidance on exclusion and restricted leave, see the Asylum Instruction on Exclusion under Articles 1F and 33(2) of the Refugee Convention, Humanitarian Protection and the instruction on Restricted Leave.

3. Convention reason(s)

3.1.1 Actual or imputed political opinion.
